title: The Friendship Recession Is Real — and a Standing Appointment Is How You Beat It
description: Adults with zero close friends quadrupled since 1990. The fix is not meeting more people; it is having a recurring reason to talk to one. Here is how a daily pact works.
excerpt: The share of adults with no close friends has quadrupled since 1990. Most advice says go meet more people. The research points somewhere less obvious: keep one friendship on a schedule.
keywords: friendship recession, accountability partner, how to keep in touch with friends, loneliness, daily check in with a friend, habit tracker with a friend, shared streak, staying close to friends
bodyHtml:
Most writing about the friendship recession stops at the diagnosis. The numbers are genuinely alarming, and they are worth stating plainly before we get to what to do about them.

The shape of the problem

The Survey Center on American Life has tracked a steady collapse in close friendship over three decades. The share of Americans reporting no close friends at all has quadrupled, from 3% in 1990 to 12% today. At the other end, the share reporting ten or more close friends fell from 33% to 13%. In 1990, 75% of Americans said they had a best friend; now 59% do.

The Cigna Group's 2025 report puts overall loneliness at 57% of Americans, concentrated most heavily among 30-to-44-year-olds, 29% of whom report frequent loneliness. Men now report loneliness at 42% against women's 37% — a reversal of decades of rough parity.

Why "go meet more people" misses

The standard prescription is to expand: join something, get out more, meet new people. It is not wrong, but it treats a maintenance problem as an acquisition problem.

Very few adults lose their close friendships in a rupture. They lose them to drift. Nobody decides to stop talking to the person they were inseparable from at 24; the calls just get further apart until reaching out starts to feel like it needs an occasion. The friendship does not end, it goes dormant, and the awkwardness of restarting it grows in proportion to the silence.

Drift is not a shortage of affection. It is a shortage of structure. Adult life supplies no default reason to talk to a specific person on a specific day, and without one the conversation always loses to whatever has a deadline attached.

What a standing appointment does

The friendships that survive adulthood almost always have some recurring container. A weekly squash game. A Sunday phone call. A book club that meets whether or not anyone finished the book. The activity is rarely the point. The point is that it repeats, and that your absence is noticeable.

Two things happen inside a container like that. First, the decision disappears — you are not weighing whether to reach out, because the appointment already exists. Second, someone notices when you skip. That noticing is the part most people underrate. It is not pressure so much as evidence that you are accounted for.

The American Society for Training & Development's long-cited figures on commitment put the effect in stark terms: a goal that stays an idea in your head gets followed through roughly 10% of the time, while a goal with a specific accountability appointment attached reaches about 95%. Those numbers describe goal completion, not friendship, but the mechanism is the same one. A commitment with a named person and a fixed time behaves completely differently from a commitment you hold privately.

Building the container without scheduling a weekly call

A recurring call is a high bar. It needs an hour, a shared free evening, and both people in the mood at the same moment. Most adult friendships cannot clear that bar reliably, which is why the standing call so often dies within a couple of months.

A daily check-in is a much lower bar, and it turns out to be enough. Pick one thing you are both trying to do — walk, read, stretch, get to bed before midnight, practise an instrument. Commit to it together. Each of you sends a photo or a line of text as proof, every day.

What that produces is not a habit tracker with a social feature bolted on. It is a small, permanent reason to appear in each other's day, attached to something you both wanted anyway. The habit gives the friendship a container, and the friendship gives the habit its teeth.

Why the streak has to be shared

This is where most habit apps get the incentive backwards. A private streak is a number you are keeping for yourself, and a number you keep for yourself is a number you can quietly forgive yourself for breaking. Nobody else knows it happened.

When the streak belongs to both of you and a missed day resets it for both, the calculation changes completely. You are not protecting a personal score. You are declining to be the reason your friend loses theirs. That is a far stronger motivation than self-discipline, and it is available on days when self-discipline is not.

It also means the app cannot be configured into uselessness. A solo tracker with optional accountability is, in practice, a solo tracker — the optional part is the first thing to go in a bad week. If a pact cannot exist without a second person, there is no version of it where nobody notices you stopped.

The realistic claim

A daily pact will not manufacture a close friendship out of nothing, and it is not a substitute for seeing people. What it does is stop an existing friendship from going quiet, which — given that quiet is how nearly all of them end — is most of the battle.

If there is someone you have been meaning to catch up with for months, the useful move is not to schedule the catch-up. It is to find one small thing you are both trying to do anyway, and start doing it on the same days.
author: Zack Anselm

title: Showing Up Regularly Is the Whole Game
description: Run clubs and book clubs work for a reason that has nothing to do with running or books. What third places teach you about building a habit that survives a bad week.
excerpt: The third-place revival is usually told as a story about places. Look closer and it is a story about repetition — and about people who notice when you are missing.
keywords: run club, book club, third place, showing up consistently, building consistency, habit consistency, accountability partner, daily check in, community habits
bodyHtml:
Run clubs are booming. So are book clubs, climbing gyms, community kitchens and every other format where a group of people agrees to be in the same place on the same evening. Among adults aged 18 to 25, 61% now report wanting more in-person connection, and creators sold five times more tickets to live events in 2025 than the year before.

This is usually framed as a story about places — the return of the third place, the café and the park and the community centre reclaiming ground from the feed. That framing is fine, but it misses the mechanism. What makes these formats work is not where they happen. It is that they happen again.

The thing run clubs have that your running app does not

Consider what a run club actually provides. Not coaching, usually. Not equipment. Not even particularly good running — group pace is a compromise and everyone knows it.

What it provides is a fixed time, a group that expects you, and the mild social cost of not turning up. Take those away and you have a solo run, which is a thing people are dramatically worse at doing consistently despite it being easier in every logistical respect.

The same asymmetry shows up everywhere. People who cannot maintain a home stretching routine will not miss a Tuesday yoga class. People who abandon reading lists finish the book club book. The activity is identical. What differs is whether anyone would notice its absence.

Repetition beats intensity

Third places are also a useful corrective to how most people approach habits, which is to start big. A new routine typically launches at maximum ambition — six days a week, an hour a session — and that version survives contact with one difficult week before collapsing entirely.

Clubs do not work that way. A run club meets once a week, at the same time, more or less forever. Nobody is trying to peak. The whole design assumes ordinary weeks, tired participants and imperfect attendance, and it keeps running through all of them. Over a year that unremarkable cadence produces far more actual running than an ambitious plan that lasted three weeks.

The transferable lesson is to set the bar at what survives your worst week rather than what impresses you on your best one. A ten-minute commitment you keep for a year beats an hour-long one you keep for a fortnight, and it is not close.

The part that does not scale

There is an obvious limitation. A club needs a critical mass of people, a location, a time that works for a group, and someone willing to organise it. Plenty of people do not have one nearby, cannot make the time reliably, or are trying to build something — sleeping properly, practising an instrument, keeping up with a language — that no local group exists for.

So the question worth asking is which ingredient is actually load-bearing. It is not the venue, and it is not the group size. Strip a club down to the minimum that still produces the effect and you are left with two things: a repeating commitment, and at least one other person who registers whether you kept it.

Two people clear that bar. A group is a nice-to-have.

A two-person third place

That is the whole idea behind a pact. You and one other person pick a habit, commit to it together, and check in daily with a photo or a short note as proof. You share one streak, and if either of you misses a day it resets for both.

Every mechanism the run club relies on is present. The commitment repeats without being renegotiated. Somebody notices immediately when you skip. The bar is low enough to survive an ordinary week. And the shared streak supplies the thing a solo tracker structurally cannot — a cost to missing that lands on someone other than you.

What it does not require is a venue, a schedule that works for six people, or anyone to organise anything.

This is not an argument against going outside

To be clear: if there is a run club near you and you can get to it, go. In-person groups do things a phone cannot, and the research on loneliness is unambiguous that physical presence matters in ways digital contact does not fully replace.

The point is narrower. The reason those groups work on you is available in a much smaller package, and that smaller package works on Tuesdays when you cannot get across town, on the habits no club exists for, and with the friend who moved away three years ago.

Showing up regularly is the whole game. A group is one way to arrange it. One person who is counting on you is another, and it fits in a pocket.
author: Zack Anselm

title: Why Habits Stick When Someone Else Is on the Hook
description: Solo habit tracking fails for a reason that has nothing to do with willpower. What the research on social habits says about why a second person changes the outcome.
excerpt: Most habit trackers treat accountability as a feature you can switch on. The evidence suggests it is closer to the load-bearing wall.
keywords: habit tracker with accountability partner, why habit trackers fail, social habits, accountability partner app, shared streak, building habits with a friend, habit tracking motivation
bodyHtml:
Almost everyone who has used a habit tracker has the same story. The first two weeks are great. The streak counter climbs, the checkmarks are satisfying, and it genuinely feels like something has changed. Then a bad day arrives, the streak breaks, and the app quietly becomes another icon you stop opening.

The usual explanation is willpower — you did not want it enough. That explanation is both unkind and, judging by how universal the pattern is, wrong. Something structural is going on.

The private-streak problem

A solo habit tracker asks you to be three people at once: the one who makes the commitment, the one who does the work, and the one who holds you to it. The third role is the one that fails, and it fails predictably, because the person holding you accountable is also the person best positioned to grant an exemption.

You know exactly how tired you are. You know the week has been unreasonable. You are an extremely sympathetic judge of your own case, and on the night it matters you will rule in your own favour. Nothing about that is a character flaw; it is what happens when the referee and the player are the same person.

The American Society for Training & Development's widely cited figures on commitment describe the gap this creates. A goal held privately as an intention is followed through about 10% of the time. A goal with a specific accountability appointment — a named person, a fixed moment — reaches roughly 95%. Whatever the precise numbers, the direction is not subtle, and it is not about wanting it more.

What the social-habits research actually shows

There is a broader shift underway in how people structure their social lives, and it points the same direction. A 2025 Oregon State University study of more than 1,500 adults found that people in the top quartile of social media use were more than twice as likely to report loneliness — and the pattern held whether they used it in long sessions or in dozens of quick checks. The American Psychological Association now puts the share of US adults describing themselves as lonely at 40%, up from 35% in 2018.

The response has not been to withdraw from technology. It has been to get more deliberate about which parts of it involve actual people. Run clubs, book clubs, cooking meetups and creative workshops are all growing, particularly among people in their twenties and thirties. The common thread is not the activity. It is that a specific group expects you at a specific time.

Habit formation and social connection turn out to be the same problem wearing different clothes. Both fail from drift. Both are rescued by a structure that repeats and a person who notices.

Why "optional accountability" is not accountability

Plenty of habit apps have a social tab. You can add friends, share your progress, join a challenge. In practice these features go unused, and the reason is that they are opt-in at exactly the moment opting in is hardest.

Sharing a streak is easy on day nine when it is going well. On day two of a bad week, when accountability would actually do something, telling someone is the last thing you want to do — so you do not, and the feature that was supposed to catch you is switched off precisely when you are falling.

Accountability that you can decline in the moment you need it is not a safety net. It is a formality.

Making the second person structural

The alternative is to build the commitment so that it cannot exist alone. Two people, one habit, one shared streak. Both check in daily with a photo or a short note as proof. If either of you misses, the streak resets for both.

That last rule is the one that does the work, and it is the one people flinch at. It sounds harsh. What it actually does is move the stakes out of your own head and into a relationship, and relationships are much better at generating follow-through than self-assessment is.

On the night you do not feel like it, you are no longer negotiating with yourself about whether the habit matters. You are deciding whether to be the reason your friend's streak goes to zero. That is an easier question, and it has a clearer answer.

Proof, not a checkbox

One more piece matters: what counts as a check-in. A checkbox is trivially easy to tick from bed, and once you have ticked one you did not earn, the whole record stops meaning anything.

Attaching a photo or a written note raises the floor just enough. It is still fast, but it requires you to have actually been somewhere or done something, and your partner sees it. The record becomes evidence rather than self-report — which also makes it far more interesting to look back on.

Choosing the habit

Two practical constraints. Pick something you can do on your worst day, not your best — a ten-minute walk that survives a brutal week beats a workout that only survives good ones. And pick something you both genuinely want, rather than one person's project that the other agreed to out of politeness; a partner who does not care about the habit will not hold you to it.

Beyond that, the specific habit matters far less than the structure around it. Almost anything sticks when someone else is on the hook, and almost nothing does when nobody is.
author: Zack Anselm
